about.title: Ceres Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Falls happen fast, but the aftermath can drag on for months. Whether the incident happened in a Mitchell Road shopping center, a Hatch Road apartment complex, or a business along Whitmore Avenue, the property owner may bear responsibility if a hazard existed and wasn't addressed. California law requires showing the owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the dangerous condition and didn't fix it or warn visitors. That's often the hardest part of these claims, since store managers and landlords rarely admit fault outright. Surveillance footage, incident reports, and photos of the hazard tend to disappear or get overwritten within days, which is why documenting everything early matters so much. LawProactive doesn't practice law ourselves; we simply connect you, free of charge, with an independent attorney in our network who can evaluate what happened, gather the evidence before it's lost, and explain your options under California's comparative fault rules.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About a Ceres Fall

items.title: Proving Notice Takes Evidence
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard. An attorney can help identify what evidence supports that, from maintenance logs to prior complaints.

items.title: Surveillance Video Doesn't Last
items.desc: Many businesses overwrite security footage within days or weeks. Acting quickly to request preservation of that video can make a real difference in your claim.

items.title: Comparative Fault Can Reduce, Not Erase, Your Claim
items.desc: Even if you're partly blamed for not seeing a hazard, California's pure comparative fault rule still allows recovery, just adjusted for your share of responsibility.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Ceres?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If your fall happened on public property, such as a city sidewalk or a government building, the deadline can be much shorter and requires a separate claims process. Because these timelines vary, it's worth talking to an attorney sooner rather than later.

items.question: What if I fell at a business on Hatch Road or Whitmore Avenue and no one wrote a report?
items.answer: An incident report isn't required for you to have a valid claim, but it does help. If no report was made, your attorney can still work with photos, witness statements, medical records, and any available surveillance footage to piece together what happened.

items.question: Will I still have a case if I was partly distracted when I fell?
items.answer: Possibly, yes. California follows a pure comparative fault system, meaning you can still recover compensation even if you share some responsibility, though the amount may be reduced accordingly. An attorney can walk you through how that might apply to your specific situation.
